about.title: Moraga Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Moraga's mix of shopping centers, wooded trails, hillside walkways, and older residential complexes near Moraga Road and Moraga Way creates plenty of spots where uneven pavement, wet flooring, or poor lighting can cause a serious fall. When a property owner in this Contra Costa County town knew about a hazard, or should have caught it with reasonable upkeep, and did nothing to fix or warn about it, California law may hold them responsible for resulting injuries. These claims often hinge on details that fade fast: a puddle that gets mopped up, a broken step that gets repaired, or surveillance footage that gets overwritten. LawProactive doesn't practice law, but we can connect you, free of charge, with an independent attorney who understands how to investigate a Moraga premises liability case, gather the right evidence, and pursue compensation on a contingency basis, meaning no fee unless you recover.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About Your Fall

items.title: Notice Is Everything
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard before your fall. An attorney can help identify prior complaints, maintenance logs, or repair patterns that establish that notice.

items.title: Evidence Disappears Fast
items.desc: Surveillance footage often gets recorded over within days, and hazards like spills or broken flooring get cleaned or fixed quickly. Acting early helps preserve the proof your claim may depend on.

items.title: Comparative Fault Doesn't Bar You
items.desc: California is a pure comparative fault state, so even if you're found partly responsible for the fall, you can still pursue compensation, though your recovery may be reduced by your share of fault.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Moraga?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a premises liability lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a public entity, such as a Moraga town facility or a Contra Costa County building, that deadline can be much shorter and requires an early formal claim. Talking to an attorney soon after your fall helps make sure you don't miss a critical deadline.

items.question: What if I fell on a trail or hillside path in Moraga?
items.answer: Moraga has a number of hillside walkways and trail connections, and liability there can depend on who owns or maintains the specific path and whether the hazard was something they should have addressed. An attorney can help sort out whether a private property owner, HOA, or public entity is responsible. These cases often require a closer look at maintenance records and any prior incident reports.

items.question: Do I need proof the property owner knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Yes, in most cases you'll need to show the owner had actual or constructive notice of the dangerous condition and failed to fix it or warn visitors. Constructive notice can be shown if the hazard existed long enough that a reasonable property owner should have discovered it. An attorney can help gather maintenance schedules, inspection records, and witness accounts to support this.
